SpaceX has outlined five contingency landing options for Starship Flight 15 as it prepares for the ship’s first tower-catch attempt at Starbase

This visualization shows how the mission can change course if the vehicle or tower does not meet the conditions required for a safe return:

1. Indian Ocean — after ascent
If the orbital insertion burn is skipped, Starship remains on its suborbital trajectory and reenters over a predetermined area of the Indian Ocean

2. North of Hawaii — early in the mission
If the flight needs to end shortly after reaching orbit, Starship returns to a designated area of the Pacific north of Hawaii

3. Off Chile — mid-mission
A separate return opportunity allows Starship to land in the eastern Pacific, far off the coast of Chile

4. Gulf offshore — catch contingency
If the tower catch is called off before final approach, Starship has an offshore landing option in the Gulf instead of proceeding with the catch

5. North of Hawaii — late in the mission
If the planned deorbit burn is skipped, Starship completes another orbit before returning to the Pacific north of Hawaii

The objective is to bring Starship home. The flight plan builds in alternatives throughout the journey, with continuous vehicle-health checks determining when to proceed

An ambitious mission, backed by carefully planned options from ascent to final approach

SpaceX has just released a new blog about Starship's upcoming 15th flight planned for Nov 13 with more info about what to expect, the significance of this flight, and their approach to safety:

"Starship is preparing to take a major step towards full reusability: bringing the Starship upper stage back to the launch site for a catch by the tower at Starbase.

To return Starship to Starbase, the spacecraft must now fly a safe trajectory that will take it over inhabited areas in northern Mexico and southern Texas to reach its launch site for catch. Like previous flight testing and the first successful mission to orbit, Starship’s flight profile for this ambitious mission is being designed with opportunities to safely end the mission early if necessary and will follow strict criteria before committing to the final phases of flight.

OUR APPROACH TO A SAFE RETURN:
On Flight 15, Starship will initially launch to a passively safe suborbital trajectory. This is the same flight profile used on Starship’s first orbital mission and ensures that any issues encountered during ascent or shortly thereafter will result in Starship reentering over a cleared area of the Indian Ocean.

After this initial ascent, flight controllers will assess the health of Starship’s systems before giving a “go” or “no-go” for orbit. If “go”, Starship will then perform an orbital insertion burn with a single Raptor sea-level engine, increasing its speed and achieving orbit around Earth.

Once on orbit, Starship will deploy its payload of Starlink V3 satellites. Three of these satellites have been modified to acquire imagery of Starship’s heatshield. This method of analyzing Starship’s heatshield has been tested on previous flights and is one of several data sources to help inform Starship’s readiness to return to the launch site on Flight 15.

After deploying its payload, Starship will then coast in orbit for another ~21 hours until its orbit aligns with Starbase for a return. During this multi-hour orbital coast, flight controllers will continuously perform manual and automated checks of Starship systems which, similar to the first orbital flight, will be intentionally conservative. They include Raptor engine health, loss of power or communications, the health of the flight computers and navigation sensors, the structural integrity of the propellant tanks and feedlines, the ability to hold tank pressure, and Starship’s ability to control its attitude.

During this prolonged coast phase, flight control teams have several options to end the mission early and return Starship to precleared areas of the Pacific Ocean if needed. These locations include early- and late-mission splashdown options around Hawaii and a mid-mission splashdown opportunity several hundred kilometers off the coast of Chile. These precleared areas, which were also used during Flight 14, provide a safe place to land Starship if any conditions arise that may preclude the ability to perform a safe reentry.

WHAT SHIP CATCH WILL LOOK (AND SOUND) LIKE:
Flight controllers will only permit Starship to return to Starbase if the vehicle’s status meets our internally developed, and FAA-approved, conditions for a return to launch site and catch.

If these requirements are met, Starship will perform a deorbit burn with a single Raptor 3 engine. This deorbit burn will alter Starship’s path to place the vehicle on a course to reenter Earth’s atmosphere at a specific point over the Pacific Ocean, thousands of kilometers uprange from Starbase.

During reentry, Starship can alter its flight path by moving its four control flaps. This will permit Starship to maintain a safe and known trajectory while guiding itself with high precision control toward Starbase. This control will also allow Starship to carry out a series of small turns in its trajectory to intentionally fly over sparsely populated areas of northern Mexico and southern Texas.

As Starship approaches Starbase from the west, the vehicle will weave its way around the major cities in the Rio Grande Valley, passing to the north of South Padre Island and out over the Gulf of America as it makes its final turn south towards Starbase. This banking maneuver has been demonstrated several times on previous Starship flight tests.

During this phase, residents of Cameron County and those in the nearby area may hear one or more sonic booms as Starship approaches the launch site. A sonic boom is a brief, thunder-like noise a person on the ground hears when an aircraft or other vehicle in the area flies faster than the speed of sound. The sonic boom does not present a health risk and what people experience will depend on weather and other conditions.

As Starship arrives over Starbase, it will perform the final bellyflop maneuver down towards the tower at Pad 2. This bellyflop was proven during a series of high-altitude test hops and during numerous suborbital flight tests. Shortly before reaching the tower, Starship will ignite its three sea-level Raptor engines and flip itself vertical while stowing its flaps. After the flip is complete, Starship will down-select to two Raptor engines and maneuver between the tower's mechanical arms, before down-selecting to a single engine as it comes to a near hover. The arms will close rapidly to catch Starship on its two catch fittings just below the forward flaps. Once Starship registers contact with the tower arms, it will shut down its final Raptor engine.

During reentry, flight controllers will have several options to end the reentry early and safely by intentionally tumbling Starship to ensure that it breaks up in the atmosphere before reaching land. There is also a late-reentry option to send Starship into the Gulf of America if any of its systems or the tower itself encounter an issue after reentry that would preclude a safe catch at Starbase.

THE HOLY GRAIL OF ROCKETRY:
Recovering an entire orbital launch system has never been done, and Starship has always been designed change that. This full recovery is often referred to as the Holy Grail of rocketry as it enables full and rapid reuse of a rocket – opening the door to airplane-like cadence where a vehicle flies again rapidly.

Reaching this milestone with Starship will allow SpaceX to unlock the true capability of Starship and will enable future missions to establish a permanent human presence on the Moon, expand the worldwide Starlink network, launch our Starmind supercompute constellation, extend the light of consciousness to the stars, and make life multiplanetary."

天呐，海底光缆统治世界的时代要结束了，又要见证历史了🤯。。
马斯克首次公布 Starlink V4 的极端参数：性能直接跳涨一百倍，光速天然快了一点四倍且不用绕大陆架，上千万条激光链路正在把地球通信主干搬上深空。

绝大多数人至今依然以为，星链只是给偏远山区、游艇和飞机提供网络补丁的边缘工具。
直到马斯克刚刚在最新的投资人会议上摊开底牌，很多人才第一次看懂 SpaceX 真正的阳谋：把构筑人类现代文明的海底光缆网络，从大洋深处连根拔起，彻底搬到太空。
这里藏着一个极度反直觉的物理常识： 光在太空真空中的传播速度，比在玻璃光纤里整整快了 40%。
 更致命的是几何路径的差异。海底光缆必须顺着大陆架和海沟蜿蜒曲折地绕远路，而太空中的卫星激光链路，两点之间永远是沿着大圆航线在真空中直线对穿。这意味着在跨洋超长距离通信上，太空激光的延迟天然比地面光缆更低。
而阻碍这件事过去的唯一瓶颈，是带宽密度。
马斯克这次直接给出了技术迭代的量化终局： 从 V2 到即将落地的 V4 卫星，单星吞吐能力将直接迎来 100 倍的暴力跃升。 在更长期的宏大蓝图里，超过 10 万颗卫星组成的轨道阵列，每颗都将配备大约 100 个传输速率超 10 Tbps 的光学激光器，在地球外围织成一张百 Exabit 级别的无缝高速网状路由。
这已经不是在做卫星宽带了，这是在用火箭把全球互联网的核心骨干网整个重写一遍。
海底光缆容易被地质地震震断、被船锚挂伤，更深陷地缘博弈的物理封锁；而悬在头顶的真空激光网络，既没有折射损耗，也没有无法逾越的地理边界。
人类用了上百年时间，把铜线和光纤一根根沉入海底来连接彼此；而未来的文明动脉，注定要在没有阻力的星空里以光速奔流。

SpaceX just released a detailed blog post explaining how Starship will return to Starbase for its first tower-catch attempt on Flight 15

and it is going to be the first full recovery of an orbital launch system

The mission brings together both sides of Starship’s future: delivering a major payload to orbit and bringing the entire launch system home for reuse.

Super Heavy will return minutes after liftoff, while Starship will deploy 26 Starlink V3 satellites, fly a mission of more than 22 hours, then make its way back through the atmosphere toward the tower at Starbase, provided it passes the required vehicle-health checks

The update walks through the orbital safety checks, heatshield inspections, alternative splashdown locations, the precise approach over northern Mexico and southern Texas, and the final sequence of bellyflop, engine ignition, flip and catch

Flight 15 is targeting launch as early as Friday, November 13, pending regulatory approval. The 75-minute launch window opens at 4:45 p.m. CT. Here is the full plan, from liftoff to bringing both stages home

1. LAUNCH AND THE BOOSTER’S RETURN

Super Heavy will lift Starship from Starbase before the vehicles separate through hot-staging: Starship ignites its engines while still attached, then continues toward space as the booster turns back.

The booster will perform its boostback burn, descend toward Starbase and begin its landing burn roughly six minutes after liftoff. The catch is planned for approximately 6 minutes 35 seconds into flight.

This will be the first catch attempt for a V3 Super Heavy booster. SpaceX has already caught three V1 boosters, with two subsequently flown again.

2. THE HARDWARE DESIGNED FOR CATCHING

Super Heavy V3 has three grid fins instead of four. Each is 50% larger and significantly stronger, with a new catch point and revised positioning to support lifting and catching operations.

The tower’s mechanical arms......the chopsticks are shorter to allow faster movement and better tracking during a catch. Their main actuators have changed from hydraulic to electromechanical, improving speed, redundancy and reliability

These changes are part of the broader V3 architecture, designed around making recovery and reuse routine operations.

3. STARSHIP DOES NOT COMMIT TO ORBIT IMMEDIATELY

The ship initially follows a passively safe suborbital trajectory rather than entering a sustained orbit directly.

This is deliberate. If a problem occurs during ascent or shortly afterward, the trajectory takes Starship toward a cleared reentry area over the Indian Ocean without requiring a successful orbital mission.

After ascent, flight controllers assess the vehicle’s health and make a go/no-go decision for orbit.

With a go, one sea-level Raptor performs an orbital insertion burn approximately 26 minutes after liftoff, increasing Starship’s speed enough to establish orbit.

4. DEPLOYING 26 STARLINK V3 SATELLITES

Satellite deployment is planned to begin around 35 minutes into flight and finish around 1 hour 18 minutes.

Each Starlink V3 satellite adds approximately 1 terabit per second of network capacity. SpaceX compares this mission’s 26 satellites with roughly 10 Falcon 9 launches carrying V2 Mini satellites.

After deployment, the satellites unfold their antennas and solar arrays, establish radio and laser communications, and use onboard propulsion to raise their orbits. Customer service is expected to begin as soon as a few weeks after launch.

Three satellites have an additional job: photographing Starship’s heatshield.

Those images will be transmitted to operators and become one of several sources of information used to assess whether the ship is ready to return to Starbase. SpaceX has already tested this inspection method on previous flights.

5. ALMOST A DAY IN ORBIT

The planned mission lasts more than 22 hours, with approximately 14 orbits at an altitude of roughly 275 kilometers.

After deploying the satellites, Starship will coast for around another 21 hours until its orbit aligns with Starbase for the return.

Throughout that period, controllers will run continuous manual and automated checks. These cover engine health, power, communications, flight computers, navigation sensors, tank and feedline integrity, tank pressure and attitude control......the ability to maintain the ship’s intended orientation.

These checks are intentionally conservative. Returning to the tower is something the vehicle must qualify to do through its condition in flight.

6. ALTERNATIVE RETURN OPTIONS THROUGHOUT THE MISSION

The flight includes opportunities to end the mission early in precleared Pacific Ocean areas if the vehicle is not suitable for a Starbase return.

These include early- and late-mission splashdown options around Hawaii and a mid-mission opportunity several hundred kilometers off Chile’s coast. The same areas were used during Flight 14.

The mission therefore has multiple decision points rather than a single commitment to return home regardless of the vehicle’s condition.

7. THE DEORBIT BURN AND REENTRY

Starship will proceed toward Starbase only if it meets SpaceX’s internally developed, FAA-approved conditions for return and catch.

A single Raptor 3 engine will perform the deorbit burn, planned around 21 hours 36 minutes after launch. That changes the ship’s trajectory toward atmospheric entry over the Pacific Ocean, thousands of kilometers uprange from Starbase.

Reentry is planned to begin around 22 hours 11 minutes into flight.

The four control flaps will guide Starship along its intended trajectory while allowing small, deliberate turns to route it over sparsely populated areas of northern Mexico and southern Texas.

8. THE FLIGHT PATH BACK TO STARBASE

Starship will approach from the west and steer around the major cities of the Rio Grande Valley.

It will pass north of South Padre Island, continue out over the Gulf, then make its final turn south toward Starbase.

This is not an entirely untested maneuver: SpaceX has demonstrated the banking maneuver on previous Starship flights.

Residents of Cameron County and nearby areas may hear one or more sonic booms. What people experience will depend on weather and other conditions.

Reentry over land also has extensive spaceflight precedent, including the Space Shuttle, Dragon’s previous Florida returns, and Soyuz and Shenzhou missions.

9. HOW EARLIER FLIGHTS PREPARED THE HEATSHIELD

Previous ocean-return tests allowed SpaceX to deliberately push the heatshield, structure and control systems beyond the demands of a normal return to the launch site.

Experiments included removing dozens of heatshield tiles from critical locations and flying maneuvers that subjected the vehicle and flaps to higher heating and aerodynamic forces than a nominal reentry.

Flight 15 also retains Flight 14’s heatshield improvements, including additional tile-retention mechanisms in vulnerable areas, measures addressing plasma intrusion behind tiles, and curved tiles across a large portion of the shield to reduce heating between them.

The V3 rear-flap mechanism uses a single actuator with three motors per flap, improving redundancy while reducing mass and cost.

10. THE FINAL BELLYFLOP, FLIP AND CATCH

Arriving over Starbase, Starship will descend toward the tower at Pad 2 in its bellyflop orientation.

Shortly before reaching the tower, it will ignite its three sea-level Raptors, flip upright and stow its flaps.

Once vertical, it will reduce to two engines and maneuver between the tower’s arms. It will then reduce to one engine as it approaches a near hover.

The arms will close rapidly around two catch fittings just below the forward flaps.

Once Starship detects contact with the arms, it will shut down its final engine.

The ship catch is planned for approximately 22 hours 32 minutes after liftoff. All mission timings are approximate and subject to change.

11. SAFETY OPTIONS REMAIN AVAILABLE DURING REENTRY

SpaceX has built in options to end reentry before the ship reaches land if necessary, including intentionally tumbling the vehicle to ensure atmospheric breakup.

There is also a late option to divert into the Gulf if either the ship or the tower develops a problem that prevents a safe catch.

The objective is ambitious, but the return is governed by explicit vehicle-health requirements and multiple alternatives throughout the flight.

12. WHY THIS MISSION MATTERS

Catching the booster solves one part of the recovery challenge. Bringing the upper stage back from orbit addresses the other.

SpaceX described recovering the entire orbital launch system as the “Holy Grail of rocketry” the foundation for full and rapid reuse and an eventual airplane-like flight cadence.

That is the capability behind Starship’s larger mission: expanding Starlink, deploying the planned Starmind supercompute constellation, establishing a permanent human presence on the Moon and making life multiplanetary.

Flight 15 is taking SpaceX another major step toward that future: launch, deploy, orbit, return and bring both stages home

SpaceX’s Arizona data center, per a county supervisor: “We could be reducing property taxes across the board in Cochise County, the entire county, by 20%”

Frank Antenori, whose district includes the site, brought up the county’s tax math during a live Q&A:

“Here’s just something to just chew on. Arizona has an expenditure limit requirement that is placed on counties. If we exceed that expenditure, we have to rebate back to the taxpayers a certain amount.”

“So, if we’re receiving revenue in from SpaceX, by law, we have to offset that to the taxpayers. We have the potential to reduce, based on the projected revenue they’re creating, as much as 20%.”

“Let me just say it again. We could be reducing property taxes across the board in Cochise County, the entire county, by 20% to offset for the revenue here, because we can’t spend all that money. So, we have to give that money back to the taxpayers. The law says we have to.”

“So, you could see a potential significant impact to local property taxes. What that is, I don’t know. We’re going to have to do the math on it. But the law, if we have this large increase in property tax revenue, we have to balance those rates. So that will reduce dramatically the property tax burden of every resident in the county.”

“The construction sales tax, which also is the TPT, the transaction privilege tax, the retail tax, and the jail excise tax. So that will be part of the construction tax. We could literally use that money to pay the jail off in 2 to 3 years, as opposed to the 13 to 20 years.”

“So this could be a revenue to eliminate the half-cent sales tax in 2 to 3 years. We can get rid of that half-cent sales tax.”

posts.text:
Grok Build packed a serious upgrade into this release, making multi-agent workflows more reliable, easier to control, and much smoother to manage

Background agents and workflows now stay visible as active work on the dashboard, workflow status shows how many agents are still running, and stop controls work even when approval prompts are open. Permission rules that fail to load now trigger warnings instead of silently being ignored

Session recovery is also more reliable, manually saved file edits are better protected, and Ctrl+L can now quote selected messages directly into your prompt. There’s also improved keyboard navigation, better terminal compatibility, and fixes across skills, hooks, file handling, and session management

Another strong push toward making Grok Build a dependable environment for running entire teams of AI agents

Release Notes: v1.0.75

Features:

• Permission rules that don't load, such as a rule that doesn't parse or a .claude/settings.json that isn't valid JSON, show a warning when a session opens instead of being skipped silently.
• Cmd+Up / Cmd+Down and Ctrl+Home / Ctrl+End move the cursor to the start or end of the whole prompt, and with Shift they select to there.
• Send now shows as Enter Enter in the footer where Ctrl+Enter arrives as plain Enter, such as inside tmux with its default settings.
• Esc on a /btw side question that hasn't been answered yet cancels it, instead of letting it run on and reopening the panel when the answer arrives.
• Clicking a link or file that can't open, such as over SSH with no display, shows why, for example "Can't open links over SSH".
• Left on an empty prompt opens the dashboard from any session or the welcome screen, not only from a session you opened from the dashboard.
• The /btw question in the panel's title can be selected with the mouse and is copied to the clipboard when you release, like the answer text.
• Workflow status lines say how many agents are still running instead of how many exist.
• Ctrl+L in the scrollback adds the selected message or highlighted text to the prompt as a quote. Open Extensions with /plugins.

Bug Fixes:

• Notes above a queued prompt, such as a model switch result or a ready worktree, stay on screen when the prompt starts instead of scrolling out of view.
• Stop buttons in the dock stop a background run while its approval card is open, instead of doing nothing until you answer the card.
• Rejecting a change keeps edits you saved to the file yourself, even when Grok missed the save, instead of overwriting them.
• grok --resume <id> opens the session in the folder it was recorded in, wherever you launch Grok from, instead of refusing.
• Windows: on older consoles such as plain cmd.exe and Windows PowerShell windows, the ▶, ⏸ and ◌ marks in todo, workflow and list rows show as characters the console can draw instead of empty boxes.
• Generated image and video paths with wide characters such as Chinese, Japanese or emoji fit their row and keep the file name, and Windows paths keep it too.
• The rewind confirmation no longer crashes Grok on a short terminal or when you shrink the window while it's open.
• Footer and status bars in narrow terminals drop or shorten the items that don't fit, instead of painting them over each other or cutting buttons off.
• Cut-off Fetch, Web Search and MCP tool output ends with the same … +N lines · <key> to view all row as code cells, naming your viewer key, and one hidden line reads +1 line.
• 16-color terminals show the paste label and tool accents in the muted gray other secondary text uses, and the paste label's brackets no longer vanish on the light theme.
• A question card's Enter:submit button, the dashboard session popup's [✗] and collapsed workflow rows highlight under the mouse pointer like other clickable controls.
• Emoji and keycap symbols such as ⚠️ or #️⃣ are measured at the width the terminal draws them, so rows no longer run past their box or lose their ….
• /export to a named pipe that nothing is reading fails right away instead of freezing Grok until it is killed.
• Typing a digit or symbol while the scrollback has focus, with vim keys off, moves focus to the prompt and types it there, as letters already do. ? still opens the command palette.
• grok sessions delete no longer fails with "Directory not empty" when another process is still writing into the session's folder.
• Dashboard rows stay in Working while a session's background subagents or workflow runs are going, and stopping the row ends them.
• Code blocks inside quotes render every line under the quote's bars, quote copies turn reference links into inline links, and lines after multi-line math are numbered correctly.
• Disabling a project's hook in /hooks applies only to that repository, instead of also skipping hooks with the same name in other repositories.
• Turning a skill on or off in the Skills tab saves only [skills].disabled to config.toml, so an organization's managed skill folders and ignore list keep applying.
• /btw starts a side question only when it begins the message. A /btw later in the text goes to the main conversation as typed.

quote.name: X Freeze
quote.text:
Grok Build just got a massive performance and reliability upgrade, with improvements across multi-agent workflows, terminal responsiveness, session recovery, and overall stability

Long-running sessions now use less memory, large JSON and log pastes no longer freeze the terminal, Linux file watching uses significantly less CPU, and background subagent activity triggers far fewer unnecessary screen redraws

Session resuming is also much faster, subagent conversations are easier to follow, shell approvals now explain why commands were blocked, and `@` file navigation can access files outside the workspace

There’s also a huge reliability pass covering safer updates, MCP authentication, context window handling, workflow execution, Windows and macOS stability, and more reliable headless sessions

Grok Build keeps getting better at handling bigger projects, longer conversations, and increasingly complex multi-agent workloads without slowing down

Release Notes: v1.0.74

Features:

• Messages between subagents appear as left-aligned rows under the bullet that name the sender and recipient, replacing the centered rows
• Shift+Enter inserts a newline in VS Code and other xterm.js-based terminals that use the Kitty keyboard protocol
• `/mcps`: when a browser can't open an MCP server's sign-in URL, the URL shows in a panel you can copy with `c` or the [Copy the url] button
• [Copy] button in a finished `/btw` panel and its folded transcript row copies the whole answer, even when only part of it is visible
• Shell approval cards say when Auto-review blocked a command or couldn't review it, and Ctrl+F shows the reviewer's explanation
• `!` mode Tab completion offers commands installed as symlinks, such as Homebrew, npm, rustup and Debian alternatives binaries
• Quotes in replies get a [Copy] button that copies the whole quote as Markdown without its `>` markers
• Named subagent links open on a plain click, so they work over SSH from macOS where a modified click can't reach Grok
• `@` paths outside the workspace: an `@` path that starts with `/`, `~/` or `../` lists files from that folder; set `[ui] at_picker_outside_workspace = false` to turn it off.
• Picked `@` files in the prompt can be edited in place: Backspace at the end of one reopens the picker on its path, and Left or Right puts the cursor inside it to change the path

Bug Fixes:

• Built-in skills, agents and workflows are refreshed when their local cache's manifest is missing or corrupt, instead of staying outdated or failing every sync
• Ctrl+Y on a question card no longer closes it without an answer; while you type an answer, it pastes back text cut with Ctrl+K
• `/new` tabs show the context window you just switched to before the new session replies
• Resumed sessions show a background command's completion in the turn that ran it, with its real run time instead of about 0.0s
• `grok update` runs when GROK_SANDBOX, --sandbox, or config sets a sandbox profile, unless Grok is already running confined
• `/btw` on a very short terminal no longer swallows arrow keys, Page Up/Down or clicks while its panel is too small to draw
• A code block's [Copy] in the transcript copies while a queued prompt is open for editing, instead of copying nothing or closing the edit
• `grok logout` stays signed out when another running Grok refreshes its sign-in, instead of signing you back in on the next launch
• Opening links and files from the TUI no longer leaves a zombie process behind for each click
• A failed session delete shows the "Couldn't delete session" prefix once, so the reason is no longer cut off
• Windows: Grok exits fully after a startup error, a `/minimal` or `/fullscreen` switch, or a signal, instead of sometimes hanging
• Grok running confined in a sandbox never starts an update on its own and tells you to run `grok update` instead
• Quitting to install an update with Ctrl+U on the welcome screen exits within the usual exit deadline instead of sometimes hanging after "Update installed"
• `grok update --force-reinstall`, or `grok update --version` with the installed version, keeps your working Grok on Linux and macOS when the download fails its checks, instead of deleting it
• Windows installers check that the downloaded build runs before replacing grok.exe and agent.exe, and keep the existing install when it doesn't, such as when a proxy serves a blocked-download page
• Command-line arguments that aren't valid UTF-8 no longer crash Grok at startup: paths such as --cwd accept them, and text such as -p gets a usage error
• Installers keep the installed Grok when a proxy or cache returns an empty download, instead of replacing it with an empty file and reporting success
• Environment variables with non-UTF-8 bytes no longer stop Grok from starting.
• Workflow run lines in the transcript end with what the run returned instead of a bare colon, `/tasks` shows the time it was taken, and polling an unknown task id leaves a row with its error
• Headless runs stopped by Ctrl+C or SIGTERM end their json, streaming-json or streaming-messages-json output with a closing record that keeps the run's outcome, instead of cutting off the stream
• macOS: the TUI no longer freezes when it runs inside a sandbox that blocks the window server
• `grok -p --resume` shows why a session couldn't load instead of always "Session does not exist", and with `--output-format json` a resume, continue or fork that fails before the session opens prints one JSON error
• Sessions with an unrecognized reasoning effort or unreadable bytes in their history resume instead of failing: the session runs at the model's default effort and says so once, and the unreadable lines are left out of the transcript
• Windows: on older consoles such as plain cmd.exe and Windows PowerShell windows, status marks and selection arrows in workflow views, the dashboard, and the feedback and extensions dialogs show as >, ·, √ or x instead of empty boxes
• File paths with spaces in inline code, such as `~/Library/Application Support/...`, link to the whole path when it exists instead of stopping at the first space.
• Feedback that can't be sent leads with the outcome, such as "Couldn't send feedback. Saved to Drafts.", then gives the reason and says to retry from `/feedback`.
• Dialog tab labels, shortcuts and settings rows that don't fit end in … instead of being cut off
• Prompt history search highlights matched letters in the same color as other fuzzy lists, and the counts on the `/` and `@` menu borders are dimmed like other border captions
• Dashboard: the peek header reads Responding while a reply streams, and the Esc footer hint reads new agent like the other lowercase hints
• Custom agent files saved with a UTF-8 byte order mark, as some Windows editors write them, load instead of being skipped
• Running markers in workflow views and MCP servers that are still starting use the theme's running color, like other progress indicators
• Minimal mode: "Sign-in failed" shows in the error color instead of the warning color.
• Context window: a larger window picked with `/context-window` or set with `context_window` in a `[model."<id>"]` table stays in effect, so compaction no longer starts early after the session sits idle, after a failed request such as a rate limit, or until you restart

Performance:

• Long sessions use less memory: finished Markdown blocks far off screen release their rendered layout, and search still finds their text
• Typing no longer lags when ffmpeg isn't installed and PATH holds slow directories, such as Windows drives under WSL
• Long pastes that arrive as keystrokes, such as pastes on native Windows or in terminals without bracketed paste, no longer freeze the prompt for seconds while the plan-mode tip is on
• Pasting long single-line text such as logs, JSON or base64 into the prompt no longer freezes the TUI for seconds
• File watching on Linux no longer keeps a CPU core busy for about a minute after startup in large repositories.
• Lower CPU use while subagents run: the TUI repaints only for animations on screen, about 7 times a second instead of 30 when no running row is visible
• `grok --resume <id>` opens much faster on large session stores, reading only the resumed session instead of every session

After DOGE, Elon came to a conclusion most people missed.

He tried to reform the state from the inside. He failed. And he said it plainly: the government can't fix its own deficit. Nobody in power actually wants to cut. The machine protects itself.

So he drew the only logical conclusion. If the state can't be reformed, there are only two ways this ends.

Either global bankruptcy. Debt keeps compounding, interest payments eat the budget, and the system collapses under its own weight.

Or robots. AI and robotics grow the economy so fast that the debt becomes manageable, and abundance makes the old fights over scarcity irrelevant.

Here's the part almost nobody sees.

For two centuries, capitalism has had a marketing problem. Its gains are real but slow and invisible. 2% growth a year doesn't feel like anything. Your life gets better over 30 years and you never connect it to the system that did it. Meanwhile, the left's promises feel immediate and concrete: a check, a subsidy, a benefit. That's why the left wins on promises even when it can't deliver them. Capitalism produces the wealth, socialism takes the credit.

Robots break that asymmetry.

When productivity doubles in a few years instead of a few decades, people will see it. Things get cheaper, services get better, opportunities appear, in real time. For the first time in history, people will connect capitalism and their rising standard of living directly, almost instantly. The causal chain becomes visible.

And that changes everything politically.

So there are two scenarios.

Scenario one: we stay in the current inertia. No breakthrough, or a breakthrough we regulate to death. The debt wins. Living standards stagnate, then fall. A frustrated electorate turns to whoever promises the most, and that pushes toward a hard collectivist left. But collectivism fails, as it always does. A kid in the suburbs gains infinitely more from a booming, abundant West than from a bankrupt state handing out promises it can't keep. Abundance is the most powerful integration machine ever built.

That's the Western renaissance.

The West doesn't need to win the culture war by arguing. It needs to win it by delivering. And for the first time, it has the technology to deliver fast enough for people to notice.

The race isn't left vs right anymore. It's robots vs bankruptcy.

Release Notes: v1.0.74

Features:

• Messages between subagents appear as left-aligned rows under the bullet that name the sender and recipient, replacing the centered rows
• Shift+Enter inserts a newline in VS Code and other xterm.js-based terminals that use the Kitty keyboard protocol
• `/mcps`: when a browser can't open an MCP server's sign-in URL, the URL shows in a panel you can copy with `c` or the [Copy the url] button
• [Copy] button in a finished `/btw` panel and its folded transcript row copies the whole answer, even when only part of it is visible

• `!` mode Tab completion offers commands installed as symlinks, such as Homebrew, npm, rustup and Debian alternatives binaries

• Named subagent links open on a plain click, so they work over SSH from macOS where a modified click can't reach Grok
• `@` paths outside the workspace: an `@` path that starts with `/`, `~/` or `../` lists files from that folder; set `[ui] at_picker_outside_workspace = false` to turn it off.
• Picked `@` files in the prompt can be edited in place: Backspace at the end of one reopens the picker on its path, and Left or Right puts the cursor inside it to change the path

• Built-in skills, agents and workflows are refreshed when their local cache's manifest is missing or corrupt, instead of staying outdated or failing every sync
• Ctrl+Y on a question card no longer closes it without an answer; while you type an answer, it pastes back text cut with Ctrl+K
• `/new` tabs show the context window you just switched to before the new session replies

• `grok update` runs when GROK_SANDBOX, --sandbox, or config sets a sandbox profile, unless Grok is already running confined
• `/btw` on a very short terminal no longer swallows arrow keys, Page Up/Down or clicks while its panel is too small to draw
• A code block's [Copy] in the transcript copies while a queued prompt is open for editing, instead of copying nothing or closing the edit
• `grok logout` stays signed out when another running Grok refreshes its sign-in, instead of signing you back in on the next launch
• Opening links and files from the TUI no longer leaves a zombie process behind for each click
• A failed session delete shows the "Couldn't delete session" prefix once, so the reason is no longer cut off
• Windows: Grok exits fully after a startup error, a `/minimal` or `/fullscreen` switch, or a signal, instead of sometimes hanging
• Grok running confined in a sandbox never starts an update on its own and tells you to run `grok update` instead
• Quitting to install an update with Ctrl+U on the welcome screen exits within the usual exit deadline instead of sometimes hanging after "Update installed"
• `grok update --force-reinstall`, or `grok update --version` with the installed version, keeps your working Grok on Linux and macOS when the download fails its checks, instead of deleting it
• Windows installers check that the downloaded build runs before replacing grok.exe and agent.exe, and keep the existing install when it doesn't, such as when a proxy serves a blocked-download page
• Command-line arguments that aren't valid UTF-8 no longer crash Grok at startup: paths such as --cwd accept them, and text such as -p gets a usage error
• Installers keep the installed Grok when a proxy or cache returns an empty download, instead of replacing it with an empty file and reporting success
• Environment variables with non-UTF-8 bytes no longer stop Grok from starting.
• Workflow run lines in the transcript end with what the run returned instead of a bare colon, `/tasks` shows the time it was taken, and polling an unknown task id leaves a row with its error
• Headless runs stopped by Ctrl+C or SIGTERM end their json, streaming-json or streaming-messages-json output with a closing record that keeps the run's outcome, instead of cutting off the stream
• macOS: the TUI no longer freezes when it runs inside a sandbox that blocks the window server
• `grok -p --resume` shows why a session couldn't load instead of always "Session does not exist", and with `--output-format json` a resume, continue or fork that fails before the session opens prints one JSON error
• Sessions with an unrecognized reasoning effort or unreadable bytes in their history resume instead of failing: the session runs at the model's default effort and says so once, and the unreadable lines are left out of the transcript
• Windows: on older consoles such as plain cmd.exe and Windows PowerShell windows, status marks and selection arrows in workflow views, the dashboard, and the feedback and extensions dialogs show as >, ·, √ or x instead of empty boxes
• File paths with spaces in inline code, such as `~/Library/Application Support/...`, link to the whole path when it exists instead of stopping at the first space.
• Feedback that can't be sent leads with the outcome, such as "Couldn't send feedback. Saved to Drafts.", then gives the reason and says to retry from `/feedback`.
• Dialog tab labels, shortcuts and settings rows that don't fit end in … instead of being cut off
• Prompt history search highlights matched letters in the same color as other fuzzy lists, and the counts on the `/` and `@` menu borders are dimmed like other border captions
• Dashboard: the peek header reads Responding while a reply streams, and the Esc footer hint reads new agent like the other lowercase hints
• Custom agent files saved with a UTF-8 byte order mark, as some Windows editors write them, load instead of being skipped
• Running markers in workflow views and MCP servers that are still starting use the theme's running color, like other progress indicators
• Minimal mode: "Sign-in failed" shows in the error color instead of the warning color.
• Context window: a larger window picked with `/context-window` or set with `context_window` in a `[model."<id>"]` table stays in effect, so compaction no longer starts early after the session sits idle, after a failed request such as a rate limit, or until you restart

Performance:

• Long sessions use less memory: finished Markdown blocks far off screen release their rendered layout, and search still finds their text
• Typing no longer lags when ffmpeg isn't installed and PATH holds slow directories, such as Windows drives under WSL
• Long pastes that arrive as keystrokes, such as pastes on native Windows or in terminals without bracketed paste, no longer freeze the prompt for seconds while the plan-mode tip is on
• Pasting long single-line text such as logs, JSON or base64 into the prompt no longer freezes the TUI for seconds
• File watching on Linux no longer keeps a CPU core busy for about a minute after startup in large repositories.
• Lower CPU use while subagents run: the TUI repaints only for animations on screen, about 7 times a second instead of 30 when no running row is visible
• `grok --resume <id>` opens much faster on large session stores, reading only the resumed session instead of every session

Grok Build just got a powerful new update, turning its terminal into an even more interactive command center for multi-agent workflows.

File paths, subagent IDs, background tasks, and pull-request numbers are now clickable directly from agent replies, while workflow navigation makes it easier to jump between phases and individual agents without digging through transcripts.

One of the biggest improvements is under the hood: MCP tools built with FastMCP or the official MCP SDK no longer send duplicate results, cutting context usage for those calls roughly in half.

There are also safer session deletion prompts, better feedback handling, fixes for custom models, more reliable MCP responses, and improved terminal navigation.

Less wasted context. Faster navigation. Much better control over complex agent workflows.

Release Notes: v1.0.72

Features:

• Relative file paths in the agent's output, such as src/app/main.rs, open on click when the file exists under the session's folder, as absolute paths already do.
• Subagent and background task ids mentioned in the transcript open that subagent's view or the task's output on click.
• Pull-request numbers such as #123 in the agent's replies open that pull request on the session repository's forge.
• Subagents named in a reply show as the subagent's label instead of its raw id once the reply finishes, as a link that opens its transcript.

• Warp: clicking a URL that wraps across rows opens the whole URL instead of only its first row.
• /delete confirmation starts on Cancel, so pressing Enter no longer deletes the session; press 1 to delete.
• Max thoughts width (/settings, [ui].max_thoughts_width) sets how wide thinking blocks wrap; it previously had no effect.
• Dashboard shows the new folder on the dispatch box's top border right after a Ctrl+L or /cd pick.
• Custom models on the Responses API with a non-xAI base_url no longer fail every turn with an HTTP 400 schema error for use_tool.
• /feedback Drafts tab keeps the selected draft when the list reloads, such as after leaving Drafts and coming back.
• MCP tools built with FastMCP or the official MCP SDK send their result to the model once instead of twice, so each call uses about half the context.
